==Education==
Gilmore was educated at [[St Bede's College, Christchurch]] and the [[University of Canterbury]] (both in [[New Zealand]]), where he was awarded a Bachelor of Science degree in 1973.<ref name=whoswho/>

Gilmore remained at the University of Canterbury as a postgraduate research student. He used the 0.61-metre telescope at [[Mount John University Observatory]] to monitor changes in the brightnesses of [[quasars]] in the southern hemisphere of the sky. He measured the magnitudes of about 130 quasars from a large number of photographic plates. He found the results were best explained by the infall of gas on to supermassive black holes. This research led to the award of a PhD degree in 1979.<ref name="gerryphd">{{cite thesis |last=Gilmore |first=G. |year=1979 |type=Doctoral thesis |title=Observational extragalactic astronomy : an investigation of southern quasars and related objects |publisher=UC Research Repository, University of Canterbury |hdl=10092/7584 |doi=10.26021/6857 |url=https://ir.canterbury.ac.nz/handle/10092/7584}}</ref>

==Royal Observatory, Edinburgh==
Gerry Gilmore worked as a research fellow at the [[Royal Observatory, Edinburgh|Royal Observatory]], Edinburgh, [[Scotland]], between 1979 and 1984.<ref name=whoswho/><ref name="ioa_home_page"/> He used the expertise gained during his PhD to measure brightnesses and numbers of stars from photographic sky surveys. Working with Neil Reid with data from the [[United Kingdom Schmidt Telescope]], he found an excess of faint stars compared to standard models of the [[Milky Way Galaxy|Galaxy]] that represented the distribution of stars as two simple components. Gilmore and Reid argued the observed numbers of stars implied the existence of an additional component they called the [[thick disc]] that exists alongside the main Galactic disc and the stellar halo.<ref name="gilmorereid1983"/>

==University of Cambridge==
Gilmore moved to the [[Institute of Astronomy, Cambridge|Institute of Astronomy]] of the [[University of Cambridge]] in 1984 on being awarded an advanced research fellowship by the [[Science and Engineering Research Council]].<ref name=whoswho/><ref name="ioa_home_page"/> He used observations of [[spectrum|spectra]] of stars to study the structure of the Galaxy, particularly by measuring their [[radial velocity|radial velocities]]. Working with Konrad Kuijken, he used spectra of faint stars in the region around the [[South Galactic Pole]] obtained with the [[Anglo-Australian Telescope]] to measure the stars' radial velocities, and consequently to determine the surface mass density of the Galactic disc. They showed that there was little or no [[dark matter]] within the disc other than that part of the Galactic [[dark matter halo]] that extends through the disc. Consequently, dark matter within the Galaxy does not concentrate within the disc.<ref name="gilmore_kuijken_1989a">{{Cite journal 
  | last1 = Kuijken | first1 = Konrad 
  | last2 = Gilmore | first2 = Gerard 
  | title = The Mass Distribution in the Galactic Disc. – I A Technique to Determine the Integral Surface Mass Density of the Disc near the Sun 
  | journal = [[Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society]] 
  | volume = 239 | issue = 3 | pages = 571–603 | year = 1989 
  | bibcode = 1989MNRAS.239..571K | doi = 10.1093/mnras/239.2.571
| doi-access = free}}</ref><ref name="gilmore_kuijken_1989b">{{Cite journal 
  | last1 = Kuijken | first1 = Konrad 
  | last2 = Gilmore | first2 = Gerard 
  | title = The Mass Distribution in the Galactic Disc. – II Determination of the Surface Mass Density of the Galactic Disc Near the Sun
  | journal = [[Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society]] 
  | volume = 239 | issue = 3 | pages = 605–649 | year = 1989 
  | bibcode = 1989MNRAS.239..605K | doi = 10.1093/mnras/239.2.605
| doi-access = free}}</ref><ref name="gilmore_kuijken_1989c">{{Cite journal 
  | last1 = Kuijken | first1 = Konrad

  | title = The Mass Distribution in the Galactic Disc. – III The Local Volume Mass Density
  | journal = [[Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society]]

  | bibcode = 1989MNRAS.239..651K | doi = 10.1093/mnras/239.2.651
| doi-access = free 
 }}</ref>

With [[Pavel Kroupa]] and Christopher Tout, Gilmore determined the numbers of low-mass stars in the disc of the Galaxy, improving on previous measurements.<ref name = "kroupa_tout_gilmore1993"/>

During a survey of the motions of stars in the central regions of the Galaxy, Rodrigo Ibata, Gilmore and [[Mike Irwin|Michael Irwin]] found stars having radial velocities that were different to those of Galactic stars. They concluded that these belonged to a dwarf galaxy in the process of merging with our own Galaxy, and which is today called the [[Sagittarius Dwarf Spheroidal Galaxy]].<ref name = sag />

Gilmore has collaborated with a large number of scientists, including [[Rosemary Wyse]]. He has used observations of the radial velocities of stars in the [[dwarf spheroidal galaxy]] companions of the Galaxy to determine the relative contribution of dark matter to these systems.

In 1994 he was appointed to a [[Reader (academic rank)|readership]] in [[astrophysics]] in the University of Cambridge. In 2000 he was promoted to professor of experimental philosophy.<ref name="ioa_home_page"/>

Gilmore has had an important role in the design and scientific strategy of the [[European Space Agency]]'s [[Gaia (spacecraft)|Gaia]] spacecraft that is measuring the positions, motions and brightnesses of millions of stars in the Galaxy.

==Awards and honours==
Gilmore was elected a [[List of Fellows of the Royal Society elected in 2013|Fellow of the Royal Society (FRS) in 2013]]. His nomination reads: {{centred pull quote|Gerry Gilmore leads efforts to understand the structure and origin of [[Milky Way Galaxy|our Galaxy]]. He led a revival of [[star count|star-count analysis]] that first showed that the Galaxy possesses a [[Thick disk|"thick" disc]], and helped to show that the thick disc formed early in the [[Milky Way Galaxy|Galaxy]]'s life. Our current understanding of how the masses of stars are distributed at birth was produced by Gilmore's team. In the early 1990s with a student he obtained the still standard estimate of the mass surface density associated with the discs. This study set the pattern of future work. He pioneered the use of spectral surveys to unravel the Galaxy's history through its chemistry and established that stars in the halo of the Galaxy are chemically distinct from stars in the Galaxy's satellites, even though much of the [[Galactic halo|halo]] must consist of stars stripped from [[Natural satellite|satellites]]. In 1994 with a student he discovered the Galaxy's most important satellite after the [[Magellanic Clouds]]. As its leading UK proponent, Gilmore played a big role in selection of [[European Space Agency|ESA's]] revolutionary [[Gaia (spacecraft)|Gaia mission]]. He is the driving force behind the [[European Southern Observatory|ESO]]-Gaia survey, which has over 250 co-investigators and will obtain spectra designed to complement data from Gaia.<ref name=royal/>}}

Gilmore was awarded a Master of Arts degree and a [[Doctor of Science|Doctor of Science (ScD)]] degree from [[Clare Hall, Cambridge]] in 2002.<ref name=whoswho/>

* Watkins, L. L., N. W. Evans, Vasily Belokurov, M. C. Smith, Paul C. Hewett, Daniel M. Bramich, Gerard F. Gilmore et al. "Substructure revealed by RR Lyraes in SDSS Stripe 82." Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society 398, no. 4 (2009): 1757–1770.
* Wilkinson, Mark I., Jan T. Kleyna, N. Wyn Evans, Gerard F. Gilmore, Michael J. Irwin, and Eva K. Grebel. "Kinematically cold populations at large radii in the Draco and Ursa minor dwarf spheroidal galaxies." The Astrophysical Journal Letters 611, no. 1 (2004): L21.
* Smartt, Stephen J., Justyn R. Maund, Margaret A. Hendry, Christopher A. Tout, Gerard F. Gilmore, Seppo Mattila, and Chris R. Benn. "Detection of a red supergiant progenitor star of a Type II-plateau supernova." Science 303, no. 5657 (2004): 499–503.
